name: Save the Children (UK): programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults, spread by Save the Children UK's 2025 restricted spending by region (note 22: East and Southern Africa £46m, Asia £32m, Middle East and Eastern Europe £23m, West and Central Africa £20m) over the countries the annual report names (education in Afghanistan, Myanmar, Yemen, Nigeria and the DRC; immunisation in Sudan, Ethiopia and Nigeria; protection in Somalia and Syria; emergencies in Gaza, Sudan, Myanmar and Ukraine; livelihoods in Ethiopia, Malawi and Sierra Leone); the UK programmes about 3%. A judgment where no country split is published.
summary: Save the Children UK's programmes in 2025 (£209m of its £234m charitable spending, mostly passed to Save the Children International, which runs the country work): education in crises (£80m), emergency response (£38m, with the Start Network's pooled fund), health and immunisation (£40m), livelihoods (£20m), child protection (£17m), nutrition (£14m) and a little UK child-poverty work. It counts reach for some projects but not for each line's spending, and publishes no controlled evaluation of its own, so every branch is built from its spending and the research on its kind of work (the median effect of education programmes, mortality in crises, child mortality and immunisation, treatment of severe malnutrition, livelihood trials, mental health in conflict) with wide ranges, and every branch is discounted for missing data. It comes to about 0.22 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.04-1.1), about twice the site's global-health median and close to charityevals' Salvation Army overseas model: a third from education (later earnings), a third from treating severe malnutrition, then emergencies, livelihoods and health; the result is mostly uncertainty, judged costs per child and effects driving it. The biggest uncertainties are what each line costs per child reached and how much of a child's risk of death the health and nutrition work removes.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Save the Children UK, programmes (2025)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Education, 2025 (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025

rows.explainer: Save the Children UK's 2025 spending on education, with its share of management, administration and programme support costs (note 7(a)). Up £15m on 2024 from Global Partnership for Education grants for Afghanistan, Myanmar and Yemen (p. 48); also learning clubs in Nigeria and the DRC (Axe-Filles), and early learning in the UK.

rows.label: Rapid-onset emergencies, 2025 (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025

rows.explainer: Emergency response in 2025 (Gaza, Myanmar's earthquake, Sudan, Ukraine and others), with its share of support costs. It includes the Start Network's pooled Start Fund, for which Save the Children UK was grant custodian until October 2025 (£18.3m spent, note 22), the Humanitarian Leadership Academy's training of local responders, and, we take it, Elrha's research (below).

rows.label: Health, 2025 (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025

rows.explainer: Health in 2025, up from £36m on Gavi funding (p. 48): immunisation (Gavi-funded work in Sudan, the GSK-funded BOOST programme for 'zero-dose' children in Ethiopia and Nigeria), health workers and community health services.

rows.label: Livelihoods, 2025 (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025

rows.explainer: Livelihoods in 2025: climate-resilient livelihoods (128,700 people in Ethiopia's Afar and Somali regions), cash transfers with nutrition (Maziko, Malawi), savings groups and business skills, and child-poverty work in the UK (pp. 21-23).

rows.label: Protection and rights, 2025 (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025

rows.explainer: Child protection in 2025: services for survivors of gender-based violence and child abuse in Somalia, social cohesion in Syria (p. 48), psychosocial support in child-friendly spaces, community child-protection committees, the Safe Families approach to violence at home, and children's online safety (pp. 19-20).

rows.label: Nutrition, 2025 (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025

rows.explainer: Nutrition in 2025, down from £19.5m: treatment of acute malnutrition, including by community health workers in Somalia (p. 16), infant and young child feeding, and nutrition-sensitive social protection (Irish Aid in Malawi).

rows.label: Emergencies less Elrha's research (pounds)
rows.explainer: Elrha's research (£11.2m, the shared figure in facts/save_the_children.json) is modelled with advocacy in save-the-children-charityevals-advocacy; the accounts book it inside the thematic lines without saying which, and it funds research on crises, so we take it from this line. If part of it sits in health instead, this branch is slightly too small and health slightly too large.

rows.label: Share of the livelihoods line spent in the UK
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (5-30%): the accounts don't split UK work by theme. Anchors: the UK Impact Group is 119 of 863 staff (p. 42), much of it campaigning (in the advocacy line); restricted UK spending was £1.6m (note 22); the UK programmes are child-poverty work (Family Grants of £300 to families in crisis, the Baby Bank Alliance, community programmes in seven places, pp. 24-27), which fits livelihoods.

rows.label: Share of the education line spent in the UK
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (1-6%): early learning and play in the UK (Power of Play in Tower Hamlets, about 300 children; Listen to Learn in Belfast), small beside £80m of education abroad.

rows.label: Education abroad (US$)
rows.explainer: At the IRS's 2025 yearly average (facts/fx.json usd_per_gbp_2025).

rows.formula: edu_spend + emg_spend + hlt_spend + liv_spend + pro_spend + nut_spend + uk_spend
rows.explainer: Every charitable line but advocacy and awareness and Elrha's research, which are charityevals' Save the Children advocacy model (save-the-children-charityevals-advocacy): £209.0m. Most of it (£129.4m) is paid as grants to Save the Children International, which runs the country programmes, and £18.7m to partners such as Action Against Hunger, the Start Network and the WHO (grants list 2025); grants to the sister organisation count as the activities they fund.

rows.label: Total expenditure, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: The shared Save the Children UK figure (facts/save_the_children.json), read by both its models.

rows.label: Charitable activities, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: The shared Save the Children UK figure (facts/save_the_children.json), read by both its models.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ charitable expenditure)
rows.explainer: Spreads fundraising (£29.4m), the shops (£10.2m, about paid for by their £10m of sales) and the sub-let floor (£2.5m) over every charitable line in proportion to its cost; management and programme support costs are already inside each line. The shops are kept in, as in charityevals' other UK charities.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programmes, including overhead
Emergencies: cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Judgment $40 ($15-120): Save the Children UK publishes no count of people its emergency spending reached, only examples (water trucked to over 500,000 people in Gaza, mobile clinics for 20,000 and 47 safe spaces for 15,000 children after Myanmar's earthquake, p. 9). Reference class: charityevals' models put relief items at about $13 a person (MSF's relief distributions), mixed relief at about $170 (the Salvation Army's) and $330 (the American Red Cross's international responses); water trucking and clinics are cheap per person, cash and shelter dear.

rows.label: Emergencies: people reached (implied)
rows.explainer: Spending over the cost per person, at Save the Children UK's own cost (partners' and other funders' resources add reach not counted here, so credit isn't shared again below).

rows.label: Emergencies: cost per person reached, with overhead
Emergencies: death rate among the people reached during the crisis, without the response
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.02 (0.012-0.04) a person-year: Sphere's emergency threshold is a crude death rate of 1 per 10,000 a day (0.037 a year); the 2025 responses ran from acute crises above it (Gaza, Sudan) to protracted ones and disasters close to the baseline (Myanmar, the DRC, South Sudan), so the average sits between.

rows.label: Emergencies: death rate in the same populations before the crisis
rows.explainer: The shared crude death rates (World Bank, 2024) of two of the main response countries, the DRC and Sudan, as the normal rate the crisis adds to.

rows.label: Emergencies: share of the excess deaths the response averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1-10%): a mixed response of clinics, water, nutrition, cash and shelter, for the people it reaches, removes a small part of the crisis's extra deaths. Reference class: charityevals' relief models use 0.75% for MSF's item distributions, 3% for the American Red Cross's and 5% for the Salvation Army's; Save the Children's includes primary health care and nutrition, so it sits towards the top.

rows.label: Emergencies: years of the crisis the response covers per person
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3-12 months): emergency responses run for months; protracted ones (Gaza, Sudan) longer.

rows.label: Emergencies: deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
Emergencies: share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Judgment 45% (30-60%): crisis deaths are young, and Save the Children's responses aim at children; the family guide's range from mortality surveys. The shared age splits (facts/death_ages.json) have none for crisis deaths, and these shares move the whole result by about 2%, so they stay ranged judgments.

rows.label: Emergencies: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-40%): in crisis mortality surveys most deaths over five are of adults, and school-age children die least of any age; 20% as the family guide, 10% where adult violent deaths dominate (Gaza, Sudan), 40% where measles and malnutrition reach older children.

rows.label: Emergencies: of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-70%): crisis deaths among adults are split between working-age adults (violence, maternal deaths, epidemics) and older people (chronic disease without care); 50% as the family guide, 30% in protracted crises where older people die most, 70% in conflicts where violent deaths dominate.

rows.label: Emergencies: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death by age band (@moral_weights) × $life_value_multiplier.

rows.label: Emergencies: illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.002 (0-0.006): diarrhoea and respiratory illness averted by clean water and clinics, and injuries treated, over half a year. A moderate diarrhoeal episode weighs 0.188 for about 5 days (GBD 2019), 0.0026 DALYs, so this is about one episode averted per person.

rows.label: Emergencies: cash, food and goods delivered per person, beyond what averts deaths (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $15 ($5-40): part of each person's share (cash assistance, food, hygiene and shelter items) is valued as consumption; the clinics', water's and nutrition's value is in the deaths and illness above, so it isn't counted here too.

rows.label: PPP conversion (2017 international $ per US $)
rows.explainer: The shared factors of three of the 2025 response countries (Sudan, the DRC, Myanmar).

rows.label: Emergencies: consumption per person per year of the people reached (PPP)
rows.explainer: Judgment $700 PPP a year ($400-1,200): displaced and crisis-hit households in low-income countries, around the extreme-poverty line ($2.15 a day, $785 a year).

rows.label: Emergencies: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.explainer: The cash, food and goods on the site's one log-income scale over the time they are used: they raise consumption during the months each person is covered (years_exposed), so the gain is years_exposed × ln(1 + value ÷ the consumption of those months), the site's rule for a transfer used within a year.

rows.label: Emergencies: local price effects of goods brought in, as a share of their value
rows.explainer: A side effect: in-kind goods can depress local traders' prices and sales; cash raises prices a little where markets are thin. Judgment -5% (-15% to 0) of the goods' value; most of the response is services, so the effect is small.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, emergencies deaths and illness averted
rows.explainer: 0.75 (0.5-1), for the deaths and illness averted only: beyond the missing data, the share of deaths averted rests on no trial of a mixed response; the Start Fund's grants go to other agencies' rapid responses, with the same uncertainty. The goods' value is their cost, which needs no effect study, so it isn't discounted here.

rows.label: Share of the emergencies outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: 65% (40-90%): UN appeals were badly underfunded in 2025 after the US cuts, so others rarely fill the gap a responder leaves; in well-covered disasters more would have come anyway. Reference class: 60% for the American Red Cross's international responses, 72% for MSF's.

rows.label: Emergencies: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (70-100%), Convention 2: reach is Save the Children UK's own spending over the full cost of a person reached, but responses also use government health staff, UN supplies (water, food pipelines) and partners' volunteers. The canonical row is the emergencies branch's; each other branch has its own share below.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Emergencies: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the goods' value
rows.explainer: The goods are valued per person at what Save the Children UK hands out (value_delivered_per_person, within its own cost per person), so UN pipelines and government staff behind the deaths averted don't enter the value counted; only partners' and volunteers' own work delivering it does. 95% (85-100%), as CARE's relief goods.

rows.label: Education: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%), Convention 2: GPE's grants are Save the Children UK's own income (in its cost), but the learning also uses government schools and teachers, community volunteers who run the clubs and families' time.

rows.label: Livelihoods: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%), Convention 2: households' own savings and labour, government extension services and the private partners (the vanilla companies in Madagascar) add to the programme's money.

rows.label: Protection: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%), Convention 2: community child-protection committees and peer educators are volunteers, and survivors' care uses government health facilities.

rows.label: UK programmes: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (70-100%), Convention 2: Family Grants and baby banks are delivered through local partners and volunteers.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (programmes delivered as funded)
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-95%), every branch: programmes run by Save the Children International with donors' audits and reporting; some money is delayed, lost to insecurity or diverted (Gaza, Sudan, Afghanistan). Reference class: 85% for MSF's relief and the Salvation Army's grants, 90% for the American Red Cross's grants to sister societies.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1 (0.85-1.1): most of the spending is restricted government and multilateral grants; an unrestricted gift pays for fundraising, support and the programmes those grants don't cover, and can't be told apart from them. No sign it pulls in more or is displaced.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, emergencies
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of people reached by the year's spending; the effect is a judgment with no trial. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, emergencies deaths and illness averted
rows.formula: emg_evidence_adj * emg_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * emg_missing_data_adj

rows.label: All adjustments combined, emergencies goods
rows.explainer: All adjustments to the goods' value: no evidence step (goods valued at their cost need no effect study).

rows.label: Health: cost per child covered for a year by immunisation and child health work
rows.explainer: Judgment $30 ($12-80): the report counts part of the line's reach: Gavi-funded vaccine supply in Sudan reached 967,434 children in 2025 and the BOOST programme about 150,000 in Ethiopia and Nigeria (pp. 7, 15, 31); $30 implies 1.7 million children for the whole line, consistent with those counts plus the community health work. The effect per child is still judged, so the branch stays thin. Anchor: routine immunisation costs about $25-50 per fully immunised child to deliver in low-income countries beyond the vaccines Gavi supplies (the Immunization Delivery Cost Catalogue's range), and community health support a few dollars a child a year.

rows.label: Health: children covered for a year (implied)
Health: yearly death rate of children under five where the work runs
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.014 (0.008-0.02) a child-year: UN IGME puts under-five mortality at about 70 per 1,000 live births in sub-Saharan Africa and higher in Somalia, Nigeria and Chad, lower in Asia; over five years that is about 0.014 a year.

rows.label: Health: share of a child's yearly mortality the year's work removes
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1-10%): vaccines against measles, pneumococcus and rotavirus and community treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria each remove a part of child deaths for those newly covered; the community packages of the Cochrane review cut neonatal mortality by a quarter where fully delivered (Lassi & Bhutta 2015, RR 0.75), but Save the Children's support mostly adds coverage to government services, so for the average child covered the share is far smaller.

rows.label: Health: deaths averted per child covered (before adjustments)
Health: value of a child death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death under five (@moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5) × $life_value_multiplier.

rows.label: Health: illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (0-30%), as direct-health's morbidity_value_ratio: illness and disability averted beside the deaths (measles complications, pneumonia episodes).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, health
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-0.9): the vaccines' and treatments' efficacy is well measured, but how much a programme's support raises coverage isn't measured here. Reference class: 0.4 for the Salvation Army's mixed health grants; Save the Children's line is more immunisation, with better evidence.

rows.label: Share of the health outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 70% (50-90%): part of the children would be reached by government services or other agencies without the support; 'zero-dose' work targets those who aren't.

rows.label: Health: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: 50% (30-80%), Convention 2: vaccines are bought by Gavi and governments and given by government health workers; Save the Children pays for outreach, training, transport and demand. Its spending is about half of the full cost of a child reached.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, health
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of children covered by the line; the effect is a judgment from trials of the vaccines and packages, not of this work. So it is counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, health
rows.formula: hlt_evidence_adj * hlt_counterfactual_adj * hlt_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * hlt_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Nutrition: share of the line spent on treating acute malnutrition
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-70%): the report describes treatment by community health workers (Somalia) beside prevention (infant feeding, nutrition-sensitive social protection in Malawi); no split is published.

rows.label: Nutrition: cost per child treated for severe acute malnutrition
rows.explainer: Judgment $200 ($120-350): community-based management of acute malnutrition costs about $100-300 a child treated with therapeutic food and delivery in the published costings; crisis settings sit high.

rows.label: Nutrition: children treated (implied)
Nutrition: deaths per episode of severe acute malnutrition without treatment
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (4-20%): children with severe wasting die many times more often than others; cohort studies put untreated case fatality from a few to over 20%, highest with oedema and in crises.

rows.label: Nutrition: share of those deaths treatment averts
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (40-80%): treated children die at about 3-5% in community programmes, against the 10% untreated above.

rows.label: Nutrition: value of a dollar of prevention, relative to a dollar of treatment
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (0-50%): infant-feeding counselling, cash with nutrition and food security lower stunting and wasting (Maziko reduced stunting by 12% in the poorest households, p. 22), far less per dollar than treating children who are already severely wasted.

rows.label: Nutrition: deaths averted per child treated, prevention included (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Deaths averted per child treated, plus the prevention spending valued at its relative worth per dollar, as extra deaths per child treated.

rows.label: Nutrition: illness and later income, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (0-40%): less illness and stunting among survivors and the later income that comes with growth.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, nutrition
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-0.9): there are no trials of treatment against none (it would be unethical); the effect rests on cohorts, and on case definitions (the Somali trial found some over-diagnosis, p. 16).

rows.label: Share of the nutrition outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 60% (40-85%): treatment coverage is low in most crisis settings (a quarter to a half of severely wasted children reached), but some treated children would have been treated by others.

rows.label: Nutrition: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: 60% (40-85%), Convention 2: therapeutic food is often supplied by UNICEF and given in government clinics; Save the Children pays for the rest of the treatment.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, nutrition
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of children treated by the line; the effect is from cohorts, not this work. So it is counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, nutrition
rows.formula: nut_evidence_adj * nut_counterfactual_adj * nut_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * nut_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Education: cost per child reached for a year
rows.explainer: Judgment $130 ($60-250): the line is mostly Global Partnership for Education grants for out-of-school children in Afghanistan, Myanmar and Yemen; GPE's accelerated grant of $20m for about 150,000 out-of-school children is about $133 a child, and the report names programmes aiming at nearly 190,000 children (p. 33), 19,000 enrolled in Nigeria's learning clubs and 12,000 in the DRC's catch-up clubs (pp. 17-18). $60 for cheap learning clubs, $250 where a grant pays for several years of schooling or construction; a school place in a poor country is about $400 a year (charityevals' Salvation Army model).

rows.label: Education: children reached for a year (implied)
Education: learning gain per child (standard deviations)

source.title: Evans & Yuan (2022), How Big Are Effect Sizes in International Education Studies?, Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, doi:10.3102/01623737221079646
source.quote: We identify a median effect size of 0.10 standard deviations on learning and 0.07 standard deviations on access among randomized controlled trials.

rows.explainer: The median effect on learning of randomised evaluations of education programmes in low- and middle-income countries, 0.10 SD; the range from school-management programmes (0.03 SD) to well-run teacher-training and remedial programmes (0.2 SD). Save the Children's own pre-post figures (half the Nigerian children reading short sentences after 13 weeks) have no control group, so they are a check, not the effect.

rows.label: Education: earnings gain per SD of learning that lasts into adult life
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-40%): a year of schooling raises earnings about 9%, and a school year in poor countries adds well under one SD of learning, so an SD of lasting learning is worth more than a year's return; adult test-score studies put it at 10-20% of earnings. The same judgment as charityevals' Salvation Army education branch.

rows.label: Education: share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (20-80%): effects of education programmes fade in the years after them, more for short catch-up programmes.

rows.label: Education: years from the programme to adult earnings
rows.explainer: Judgment 10 years (6-15): children of 6-13 in the clubs start work in 5-15 years.

rows.label: Years the income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years).

rows.label: Household members who share the income gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier), as direct-health's later-income rows.

rows.label: Education: gain in ln(consumption) per child reached, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + edu_learning_gain_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd * edu_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - edu_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × persistence) for each working year, discounted, after the wait to adult work, shared with the household.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-1): Evans & Yuan (2022) find the median effect in the smallest quarter of studies almost three times that in the largest, so programmes at scale do about 0.04-0.06 SD, roughly 0.6 of the all-study median; in conflict settings (Afghanistan, Yemen, Myanmar) schooling is often interrupted. As the Salvation Army education branch.

rows.label: Share of the education outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 85% (60-100%): the effect is against the children's alternative in the studies; the programmes target out-of-school children in crises, few of whom would have had another place.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, education
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of children for the line and no controlled evaluation; the effect is the median of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, education
rows.formula: edu_evidence_adj * edu_counterfactual_adj * edu_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * edu_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Livelihoods: cost per household reached
rows.explainer: Judgment $200 ($80-500): savings groups cost about $20-40 a member, livelihood and climate-adaptation packages with assets and training several hundred dollars, cash transfers with nutrition (Maziko) more. The Ethiopian programme reached 128,700 people (about 25,000 households) in 2025 (p. 23).

rows.label: Livelihoods: households reached (implied)
Livelihoods: people per household
rows.explainer: The shared household sizes of four countries where the livelihoods work runs (Malawi, Nigeria, the DRC, Bangladesh); Ethiopia has none in the facts.

rows.label: Livelihoods: consumption gain per household reached, share of consumption
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (0.5-8%): the meta-analysis of savings-promotion trials in sub-Saharan Africa finds a small gain (about 0.03-0.07 SD, Steinert et al. 2018); graduation programmes, which cost far more per household, raise consumption about 5-10% (Banerjee et al. 2015). Save the Children's own evaluation in Afar (families 16 times as likely to report a rising income, p. 23) is a self-report, a check rather than an effect.

rows.label: Livelihoods: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 2 years (1-4): livelihood gains fade after the programme; assets and skills keep part of them.

rows.label: Livelihoods: gain in ln(consumption) per person, discounted over its years
rows.explainer: As cash-income's recurring-gain recipe: ln(1 + gain) for each year, discounted. A share of consumption needs no PPP step.

rows.label: Deaths averted by higher incomes, as a share of the consumption benefits
rows.explainer: The cash-income family's mortality step: higher household incomes avert some child deaths (cash transfers cut under-five deaths by about 8% in Richterman et al. 2023); GiveWell's mortality effect for cash is about 0.2 of its consumption value. Judgment 0.2 (0-0.5), times your value of a life, for the livelihoods branch (as Mercy Corps' recovery and livelihoods).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, livelihoods
rows.explainer: 0.75 (0.4-1): beyond the missing data, the trials' gains are small and imprecise; as the Salvation Army livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Share of the livelihoods outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1 (0.8-1): the trials' effects are against control villages, which already had their other options.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, livelihoods
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of households for the line; the effect comes from trials of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, livelihoods
rows.formula: liv_evidence_adj * liv_counterfactual_adj * liv_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * liv_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Protection: cost per child or survivor reached
rows.explainer: Judgment $60 ($25-150): child-friendly spaces and group psychosocial support cost tens of dollars a child; case management and services for survivors of violence hundreds. The Somali programme gave 613 survivors health and psychological care (p. 19); no count for the line is published.

rows.label: Protection: children and survivors reached (implied)
Protection: share of those reached with a mental disorder

source.title: Charlson et al. (2019), New WHO prevalence estimates of mental disorders in conflict settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis, The Lancet 394:240-248, doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(19)30934-1
source.quote: The mean prevalence of mental disorders (depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia) was 22.1% (95% UI 18.8-25.7) at any point in time in the conflict-affected populations assessed.

rows.explainer: The WHO's prevalence of depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia in conflict-affected populations, 22.1% (uncertainty interval as the range). Children in Save the Children's protection work are mostly in conflict settings.

rows.label: Protection: improvement in mental health for those with a disorder (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.3 SD (0.1-0.5): meta-analyses of psychosocial interventions for children in humanitarian settings find small to moderate falls in post-traumatic stress symptoms and none consistent for depression (Purgato et al. 2018, Lancet Global Health); support for survivors of violence and case management do somewhat more for the few who get them. Children without a disorder are counted at nothing here; any gain for them is in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Protection: years the improvement lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment a year (6 months to 2 years), fading linearly: the trials measure a few months after the sessions.

rows.label: Protection: WELLBYs per child reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Share with a disorder × the improvement in SD × its years ÷ 2 (linear fade) × the shared WELLBYs per SD-year (@wellby_factors), as the wellbeing family does.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, protection
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-0.9): the trials' effects are small and uncertain, and a mental-health score to life satisfaction step (the shared WELLBYs per SD) is for adults' depression.

rows.label: Share of the protection outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 90% (70-100%): few other services exist for these children; the trials' effects are already against control groups.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, protection
rows.explainer: Thin: no count for the line and no controlled evaluation of this work. So it is counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, protection
rows.formula: pro_evidence_adj * pro_counterfactual_adj * pro_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * pro_missing_data_adj

rows.label: UK programmes: value to families of a pound spent, as a share of a pound given to them
rows.explainer: Judgment 35% (15-60%): Family Grants (£300 a family for essentials, 2,800 children in 2025) and baby banks reach families as goods; community programmes, play and evidence work are mostly staff time. Valued as the goods they are worth to families.

rows.label: UK programmes: a Family Grant (pounds)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025
source.quote: In July, we launched the Family Grants programme. Delivered through trusted partners, the programme provides £300 grants to families in crisis for essential items

rows.explainer: The size of the grant, used to turn spending into families on the log scale.

rows.label: UK programmes: family-grant equivalents (implied)
UK programmes: people per family
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 (3.5-5): families with children in poverty, often with several children.

rows.label: UK programmes: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.explainer: A grant's worth over the family's yearly consumption, at low-income families' share of UK consumption per person (the shared figure both Save the Children models read).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, UK programmes
rows.explainer: 1: goods valued at what families would pay need no effect size; the doubt is in the cash equivalence above.

rows.label: Share of the UK outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 80% (60-100%): local authorities' crisis support and food and baby banks give some families the same help.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, UK programmes
rows.explainer: Thin: the spending is a judged share of two lines and the value per pound a judgment. So it is counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined, UK programmes
rows.formula: uk_evidence_adj * uk_counterfactual_adj * uk_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * uk_missing_data_adj
